## 1. Conduct a permutation test

Conduct a permutation test to investigate the following question:

> Do homes built pre-1970 have higher average lead soil concentrations?

To perform this test, you'll need the `exide-property-covariates.csv` file found in `/courses/EDS222/data`. This file contains the year each property was built.

### Hypothesis Tests
$H_0$: homes built pre-1970 and post-1970 have the same average lead soil concentrations

$H_A$: homes built pre-1970 have higher average lead soil concentrations


### Permutation Test
```{r}
# load in data and packages
library(tidyverse)
property <- read_csv('data/exide-property-covariates.csv')
soil <- read_csv('data/exide-soil-cores.csv')
```

```{r}
# get average soil values
soil_avg <- soil |> summarize(avg_lead = mean(pb_ppm), .by = property_id)

# join tables and add 'label' column for permutation
joined <- left_join(soil_avg, property, by = 'property_id') |> mutate(before_1970 = year_built < 1970)
```

visualize raw data
```{r}
p1 <- ggplot(joined, aes(x = avg_lead, fill = before_1970)) +
  geom_histogram()

p1
```

```{r}
# count how many empty values are in the year_built col
sum(is.na(joined$year_built))
```

```{r}
# find avg lead conc for houses built before and after 1970
avgs <- joined |> 
    group_by(before_1970) |> 
    summarize(means = mean(avg_lead)) |> 
    arrange(before_1970)

dif <- avgs$means[2] - avgs$means[1] # find dif in means (hopefully its big!)
```

```{r}
# shuffle for permutation test
shuffled <- joined |> 
    mutate(shuffled_lbls = sample(before_1970)) |> 
    group_by(shuffled_lbls) |> 
    summarize(means = mean(avg_lead)) |> 
    arrange(shuffled_lbls)

shuffled_dif <- shuffled$means[2] - shuffled$means[1]

```

```{r}
# replicate shuffle 10k times to get distribution of dif of means
null_dist <- replicate(
  1e4,
  {
    # put your "shuffle once" code in here, to repeat it 10,000 times
    shuffled <- joined |> 
        mutate(shuffled_lbls = sample(before_1970)) |> 
        group_by(shuffled_lbls) |> 
        summarize(means = mean(avg_lead)) |> 
        arrange(shuffled_lbls)

    # get the difference in proportions between the two groups
    shuffled_dif <- shuffled$means[2] - shuffled$means[1]
    shuffled_dif
  }
)
```

```{r}
# graph null distribution
tibble(diff_props = null_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diff_props)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = dif)) +
  labs(title = 'Null distribution of difference in lead levels in homes built before and after 1970', x = 'lead (ppm)')
```

```{r}
pval <- sum(null_dist >= dif)/length(null_dist) 
# the proportion of null distribution values greater than or equal to the observed statistic

pval
```

Conclusion: The p value is 0, which is less than our cut off of 0.05, meaning that we reject the null hypothesis.

::: {.callout-note}

The question is about _average lead soil concentrations_. You'll need to first get the average lead soil concentration for each property, then join your result to the property covariate data to get the year the house was built.

:::

## 2. Estimate a confidence interval

Estimate a confidence interval to investigate the following question:

> How much is the difference in average lead soil concentrations between properties within 1km of a freeway and those farther away?

### Calculate observed average

```{r}
# join tables and add 'label' column for permutation
joined_freeway <- left_join(soil_avg, property, by = 'property_id') |> 
  mutate(freeway_1km = dist_to_freeway_m <= 1000)
```

```{r}
p2 <- ggplot(joined_freeway, aes(x = avg_lead, fill = freeway_1km)) +
  geom_histogram()

p2
```

```{r}
# find avg lead conc for houses built within and without 1km of the highway
avgs_freeway <- joined_freeway |> 
    group_by(freeway_1km) |> 
    summarize(means = mean(avg_lead)) |> 
    arrange(freeway_1km)

dif_freeway <- avgs_freeway$means[2] - avgs_freeway$means[1] # find dif in means (hopefully its big!)

```

### Bootstrapping

```{r}
freeway_samp_dist <- replicate(
  1e4,
  {
    resampled_freeway <- joined_freeway |>
      slice_sample(n = nrow(joined_freeway), replace = TRUE) |> 
      group_by(freeway_1km) |> 
      summarize(means = mean(avg_lead)) |> 
      arrange(freeway_1km)
      # use slice_sample to resample rows with replacement
      # summarize to get the proportions over 200 within groups
      # sort by area

    # get the difference of proportions
    boot_dif_freeway <- resampled_freeway$means[2] - resampled_freeway$means[1]
    boot_dif_freeway
  }
)
```

### Confidence Interval

```{r}
area_95ci <- quantile(freeway_samp_dist, c(.025, .975))
```

```{r}
# graph boostrapped sampling distribution with CI
tibble(diff_props = freeway_samp_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = diff_props)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = dif_freeway)) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = area_95ci[1]), linetype = 'dashed') +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = area_95ci[2]), linetype = 'dashed') +
  labs(title = 'Mean difference in lead of homes within 1km of freeway vs outside', x = 'lead (ppm)')
```

Conclusion: We are 95% confident that the true difference in mean lead concentration between homes within and outside of 1km of a freeway is between 47.28 and 109.84 ppm.

## 3. Simulate a negative result

Recall that a p-value is the probability of observing your sample _if_ the null hypothesis is true. Therefore, if you draw a sample from two groups that part of the same population, you should get a p values less than 0.05 only 5% of the time. In other words, a negative result (no actual difference) will yield a significant p-value at the 0.05 threshold in 5% of samples. This is known as the **false positive rate**.

To simulate a negative result, perform the following.

1. Define a normally-distributed population. Pick any mean and standard deviation.
2. Draw a sample of 50 observations from this population. Assign the first 25 to group A and the second 25 to group B.
3. Conduct a permutation test to investigate whether the mean of group A is greater than the mean of group B.
4. Record your p-value.
5. Repeat the simulation 1,000 times.

When you're done, verify that your p-value is less than 0.05 in approximately 5% (50) of your simulations.

```{r}
data <- rnorm(1000, mean = 5, sd = 1)
```

```{r}
pop <- data.frame(
  value = sample(data),
  label = sample(c(rep("a", 25), rep("b", 25)))
)
```

```{r}
p3 <- ggplot(pop, aes(x = value, fill = label)) +
  geom_histogram()

p3
```

```{r}
# calculate observed difference in means (a - b)
pop_avgs <- pop |> 
  summarize(means = mean(value), .by = label) |> 
  arrange(label)
pop_dif = 0
#pop_dif <- pop_avgs$means[1] - pop_avgs$means[2]
```

```{r}
p_dist <- replicate(100, 
  {
    # permutation test
    pop_null_dist <- replicate(
      50,
      {
        # put your "shuffle once" code in here, to repeat it 10,000 times
        shuffled <- pop |> 
            mutate(shuffled_lbls = sample(label)) |> 
            summarize(means = mean(value), .by = shuffled_lbls) |> 
            arrange(shuffled_lbls)

        # get the difference in proportions between the two groups
        shuffled_dif <- shuffled$means[2] - shuffled$means[1]
        shuffled_dif
      }
    )

    pval <- sum(pop_null_dist >= pop_dif) / length(pop_null_dist) # the proportion of null distribution values greater than or equal to the observed statistic
    pval
  }
)
```


```{r}
tibble(p_vals = p_dist) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = p_vals)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0.05), color = 'red') +
  labs(title = 'Distribution of p values for permutations of a null distribution', x = 'p value')
```

### try gita way (faster!)

```{r}
data <- rnorm(1000, mean = 5, sd = 1)
```

```{r}
pop1 <- data.frame(
  a = sample(data),
  b = sample(data)
)
```

```{r}
# calculate observed difference in means (a - b)
pop_avgs_dif1 <- mean(pop1$a) - mean(pop1$b)
```

```{r}
p_dist1 <- replicate(1000, 
  {
    # permutation test
    pop_null_dist <- replicate(
      1e4,
      {
        # put your "shuffle once" code in here, to repeat it 10,000 times
        comb <- c(pop1$a, pop1$b)
        samp_combined <- sample(comb)
        shuffled <- data.frame(
          a = samp_combined[1:25],
          b = samp_combined[26:50]
        )
        # calculate observed difference in means (a - b)
        pop_avgs_dif1 <- mean(shuffled$a) - mean(shuffled$b)
      }
    )

    pval <- sum(pop_null_dist >= pop_avgs_dif1) / length(pop_null_dist) # the proportion of null distribution values greater than or equal to the observed statistic
    pval
  }
)
```

```{r}
tibble(p_vals = p_dist1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = p_vals)) +
  geom_histogram() +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = 0.05), color = 'red') +
  labs(title = 'Distribution of p values for permutations of a null distribution', x = 'p value')
```
